title: What would make you play my game?

posts.author: NaMosca
posts.body:
Guys I am development my game and it use rtp, it is a open world rpg solo game with craft system (alchemy, blacksmith and more) and a story to be investigated about the main character that lost his memories (I already wrote the plot).
What can I offer to you to play my game?
what do you want of a good game with rtp graphics?  (It will be a free game)
How many hours of gameplay do you prefer? short or long?
Thank you very much.

posts.author: Arcaines
posts.body:
So, I mean this, in the nicest way possible, but don't aim to be a person pleaser by asking people how you want
them
to make your game, because everyone has their own different taste of what type of RPG you would want to make them.
What you need to do, is settle on a RPG style that your doing and find your own audience with that game.
I've had a few people tell things they don't like about my game but I kept it in, because it's a more of a personnel preference for them.
What will happen if you choose to go down this route is that you will make a game that no one will like because you tried to please everyone.
Never try to please people only yourself.

posts.author: Ms Littlefish
posts.body:
Make the game
you
want to play. Ask for feedback, but feedback has to be filtered, tailored, and in the spirit of what
you’re
trying to create. A game that suits the styles and preferences of too many people is just gonna be a mess. It’s totally fine to be niche.

posts.author: bgillisp
posts.body:
While a meme, it is accurate to what will happen to your game if you try to please everyone.
I've also seen this in action with some kickstarter funded games where it feels like they tried to please every funder and in the end got a mess that almost no one liked in the end on Steam when the final version came out.
So in short, figure out what you want to make. Then make that.

I'm not sure why any developer would be looking to appeal to
me
specifically, but okay, I'll give you the list of stuff I usually look for in an RPG Maker Game.
1.  Decently short.  Most RPG Maker games don't end up being anything above "par for the course", so I always appreciate ones that are made by developers who know "don't wear out your welcome".  The game is only as long as it needs to be to do its job and doesn't stay longer than that.  About the time I start getting bored, it wraps up.
2.  Interesting premise.  There's twenty thousand "save the world from the big bad evil guy" games.  I need a good premise to do it.  Same with saving princesses.  Finding the McGuffin.  Whatever.  I usually end up sticking with games that FEEL unique, even if they might not be.  An interesting premise is what I look for first.
3.  Interesting gameplay.  If combat or crafting or whatever else is all "every game on the market does this" and there's nothing unique or interesting about the way you tackle it... I'll usually check out.  But, it also can't feel overwhelming or shallow.  Mostly, I'm looking for the "I just played Portal for the first time" experience.  Or, "I just played Outer Wilds for the first time".  Something like that in terms of the way gameplay works and feels.  I like that feeling.  If it's "bog standard", I'll check out.  But, I do also make exceptions for games that do stuff like Earthbound did when I was a kid (basically the whole game was pretty bog standard, but it did a couple unique things that made the game feel fun and whimsical and deep... and I will forever remember the New Age Retro Hippie as a result... the trees that explode... and all the psychedelic backgrounds with weird music in combat).
4.  Feels like some love was put into the project.  I will play and enjoy games that are utterly horrible, as long as it feels like someone put their heart and soul into the project.  Because, I find value in those experiences.  I don't know why I do, but I do.  There's something quite special to me about "this game is garbage, but this person put everything they had into this experience and cared quite deeply about it" when I play it.  It's sort of like a spiritual moment, I guess.  Those games make me pretty happy to play, because what I'm getting out of them has nothing to do with story or gameplay.  It's more to do with getting to see what the person wanted to share with the world.  I quite like it.
5.  Readability.  This is more than the text used.  Color palettes, aesthetics, etcetera.  If you use colors together that basically act as kryptonite to people who aren't color blind... I am not going to give it a try.  If I look at something and can't tell what it is immediately... I'm not going to give it a try.  I expect a certain degree of "readability" in the game itself.  Anytime I stop and go "wait, what is that?", my immersion is killed.  Not a pleasant experience.

A passion project where some serious thought was put into it and into trying to make it the absolute best it could be.  With an interesting premise to get me in the door.
NaMosca said:

With RPG Maker, I generally prefer short.  Mostly because the quality of gameplay and story in these games isn't usually anything to write home about.  Somewhere between 3-5 hours in most cases.  But, if it's good, I'll settle in for considerably more (Final Fantasy Endless Nova on RPG Maker 2000 ate like 45 hours of my life... I currenly consider it the best RPG Maker game I've ever played).

posts.author: hiddenone
posts.body:
I play on lot of demos here on the forum, and sometimes I think the devs even find it useful (at least when I'm not breaking their games in new and unique ways), but take my answers with a grain of salt since they will likely be different than a lot of devs here.
What can I offer to you to play my game?
Click to expand...
Nothing you offer will make me want to play a game more (unless you're offering cash
), but begging for attention can be a turn-off to potential players. What you
can
do is make sure you're showing off the parts of the game you're proudest of: be that describing the battle system, showing off the characters and their interactions, or having pretty maps scattered through your game page. Effort into the presentation of your game can show potential players that you've put effort into your game as well.
Another option is for you to take time to play other's games and leave comments on their pages. While that doesn't mean they will or should also play your game, it does show that you want to be involved on the forum and that can mean a few more eyes on your game. More eyes means more potential players.
what do you want of a good game with rtp graphics? (It will be a free game)
Click to expand...
I just want a game that knows what it wants to do. RTP isn't a dealbreaker for me, but if the mapping is large and empty and the battles are boring then it tells me that the dev wasn't as interested in working on those. In which case, they should've focused on the parts of the game they do enjoy working on.
How many hours of gameplay do you prefer? short or long?
Click to expand...
I prefer shorter games, since I don't have lots of free time anymore. But the length of the game doesn't mean much if the story and gameplay don't match up with the length, so figure out what your game needs and let that decide the game's length.

posts.author: Eternidade_1
posts.body:
Speaking from my point of view. What would make me play your game?
Well, if it's open source and I have the engine that was used to create the game, I'll definitely play it for a while, when I'm studying the demo, to see what was done, how it was done, what I could or couldn't use.
The game could be the worst possible, if there's something interesting in it, it's worth playing. I mean, it's interesting from the developer's point of view, features, sounds, images, texts, etc.
But realize that this is a generalization because any open game available is an opportunity to play.
If it's a closed game, then you have to satisfy the public's taste.

posts.author: AquaEcho
posts.body:
OP, it may benefit you to study copywriting and/or sales pitches. Companies don't say "please check us out" or "What would it take for you to buy our product?" In fact, many times a sales pitch is a command.
For example "Join Mario on his latest adventure through the Mushroom Kingdom" or "Enter the world of GrimDarkLandia where you'll fight powerful demons". Does that not sound more interesting to you? They are selling you on an experience, a virtual adventure. Not everyone will be interested, but some people listening will think, "that sounds cool" and check it out.
